source.title: Latent Functional Maps: a spectral framework for representation alignment
source.authors: Marco Fumero; M. Pegoraro; Valentino Maiorca; Francesco Locatello; E. Rodolà

record.tranche_reason: The study measures representational similarity and tests alignment and transfer using latent functional maps, a different method from the similarity measures and alignment evidence discussed in the claim.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results on similarity comparisons, perturbed representations, retrieval, and stitching. Cited results from other work are not included. Figure 4 reports stitching accuracy across encoder combinations, datasets, and anchor counts; the rows below record the paper's aggregate textual conclusions rather than extracting individual plotted values. The similarity and retrieval values in Figure 2 and Table 2 are recorded where stated.
record.test_reason: This is mainly a methods paper (Latent Functional Maps). Some of its results still bear on the claim. Zero-shot stitching across ViT-S/B/L and DINOv2 reaches roughly 0.85 accuracy. FastText↔Word2Vec retrieval via orthogonal maps reaches MRR 0.97–0.99. Retrieval and stitching across seed-varied autoencoders works. Seed-varied CNN layers are matched by similarity. These bear on V3 and V4, and the CKA-vs-CCA contrast bears on V6. Many rows are only LFM-versus-baseline comparisons and are relinked to none.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors present LFM as a framework for comparing, corresponding and transferring latent spaces, with better sample efficiency than baselines. They note sensitivity to the number of eigenvectors, the full-correspondence assumption, and immature fully unsupervised performance.
record.recipe_differences: The study introduces a spectral functional-map framework, graph Laplacians, descriptors, and LFM similarity. Its experiments compare this framework with CKA, CCA, direct orthogonal mappings, and other transfer methods rather than reproducing the original sources' methods.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary with similarity measure (LFM versus CKA), graph distance metric (angular versus L2), descriptor choice, anchor count, and number of eigenvectors.

fits_no_version.finding: CKA degrades under separability-preserving translations of a single space, while LFM similarity stays stable. Similarly, an L2-built graph collapses under noise (MRR 0.04) while an angular graph holds (0.99).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Robustness of similarity measures to synthetic perturbations of a single representation.

fits_no_version.finding: LFM retrieval depends on the number of eigenvectors and on anchor counts. Comparisons of LFM against other mapping methods at 2–5 anchors.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sample efficiency of alignment methods; hyperparameter sensitivity of functional maps.

record.problems: No uncertainty estimates are stated. Several results are shown only in figures, including stitching accuracy and the perturbation curves. The stitching experiments do not provide numeric accuracy values in the accompanying text. The study does not test convergence with model scale or capability.
record.rows_left_out: Figure 4 contains separate plotted stitching results across datasets, encoder combinations, methods, and anchor counts; these were not individually extracted because the accompanying text reports aggregate conclusions and the flattened figure does not reliably support assigning every plotted value. Figure 9 has additional eigenvector-count points not individually transcribed. Table 2 has other anchor-count and mapping-method entries beyond those needed to record the low-anchor contrast and high-anchor result.

untested.parts: No scaling or capability sweep. Using ViT small, base and large is not analysed as a trend.
No interpretable features, neurons or circuits.
Number of neighbours and out-of-distribution inputs are not varied for the similarity measures.
No analysis of plateaus or of causes such as shared data or objectives.
Individual units versus subspaces are not examined.

missing.what: Plain orthogonal map FastText↔Word2Vec reaches MRR 0.97 at 300 anchors, and affine reaches 0.95; Linear is 0.01 at 300.
CUB retrieval across pretrained vision encoders is low for every method: best MRR 0.33–0.34 at 250 anchors, and 0.00–0.07 at 5 anchors.
Per-dataset stitching accuracies in Figure 4 (e.g. about 0.85 for CIFAR100 coarse and ImageNet at high anchor counts), plus the text's note that DINO-vs-ViT and fine-grained pairs are harder.

record.verdict_notes: This is primarily a methods paper. Evidence for convergence is incidental: that spaces are mappable at all. Most comparative rows evaluate LFM rather than the claim and are relinked to none. It cites the Platonic Representation Hypothesis and Convergent Learning but is neither source. Figure 4 values are partly readable but hard to assign to panels.

versions.untested_parts: No sweep over model size or capability, or test of alignment rising with scale across differently trained models.
No paired image-caption or other vision-language representation alignment experiment.
Tests models or autoencoders trained from different initializations, but not whether the same individual features or shared subspaces recur, nor whether individual units or bases differ.

Tests functional-map-based transfer, orthogonal mappings, retrieval, and stitching. Does not test relative representations or alignment without paired data in the general sense; some experiments use anchors or labels.
No test of recurring interpretable features, neurons, SAE features, or circuits.
Tests sensitivity to graph distance metric, descriptor choice, perturbation, and number of eigenvectors. Does not test a range of neighbour counts or out-of-distribution inputs.
Does not establish that alignment remains incomplete or plateaus, or attribute alignment to shared data or objectives rather than a common model of reality.
